title: Quantile timeout annealing + fairshare budget: experiment scratchpad
content:
Purpose
This scratchpad captures an experiment plan and early notes for a new approach to reduce tail latency without sacrificing throughput: adaptive (annealed) timeouts per-queue quantile coupled with a small, elastic fairshare budget allocator that limits batch preemption for low-priority traffic. Goal is to reduce observed P99/P999 while keeping token cost within 5% of baseline and throughput within 3%.

Background/context
We keep seeing recurring P99 spikes during mixed workloads where a small number of long-context or high-token requests push the batch formation window and cause preemption/queue starvation for latency-sensitive traffic. Previous approaches (static shorter timeouts for high-priority, strict slotting) reduce tail but cost throughput. We want to explore a hybrid: make timeouts a function of recent latency quantiles (quantile-driven annealing) and add a tiny fairshare budget per priority class that prevents an endless string of high-throughput requests from monopolizing batch slots.

High-level idea
- Compute per-queue short-term latency quantiles (sliding window, e.g., 1–5 minutes): q50, q90, q95, q99.
- Derive an annealed timeout T_q for each queue: T_q = base_timeout * f(qX) where f() grows with tail quantile. Intuition: if P95 is high, be more conservative (longer T) for throughput-sensitive queues; if P99 is high for latency-sensitive queues, reduce timeout aggressively.
- Add fairshare budget tokens per priority class (P0 latency-sensitive, P1 standard, P2 batch). Each request consumes budget proportional to batch_size_estimate; budgets replenish slowly. When a priority class drops below threshold, scheduler temporarily favors other classes until budget replenishes. This prevents long-running high-volume classes from starving small low-latency requests.

Hypotheses
1) Quantile annealing that reacts to P95 and P99 will allow us to reduce P99 for latency-sensitive queues by ~15–30% without large throughput loss.
2) A small fairshare budget (e.g., budget size = 10 estimated batch-equivalents, replenish 1 per 200ms) will prevent multi-minute tail drift from bulk classes and reduce starvation incidents by >50%.
3) Combined, latency-sensitive tail improves and overall token/unit cost changes <5%.

Experiment design (stages)
Stage A — telemetry and simulation (non-invasive)\- Implement sliding-window quantile collector + simulator that replays traces and computes what timeouts would have been, batch sizes, expected token cost. Run on 7 days of production trace (sampled) and synthetic bursts.\- Metrics: simulated P50/P95/P99, mean batch size, expected throughput, simulated preemption count.

Stage B — shadow scheduler on canary fleet\- Deploy logic in shadow mode to compute per-queue annealed timeouts and fairshare decisions without affecting live routing. Produce scores and decisions in logs to compare with baseline.\- Run for 72 hours across 2 regions (us-west1, eu-west1) on canary capacity.

Stage C — gradual rollout with control/experiment A/B\- 10% traffic: control vs experiment groups pinned by customer or route. Enable read-only enforcement for fairshare (limit applies only when experiment triggers) with automatic rollback triggers.\- Primary metrics: P95/P99 latency per-priority, throughput (tokens/s), unit cost ($/token) estimate, preemption counts, queue occupancy distribution.

Key knobs to sweep
- base_timeout values: 6ms, 12ms, 25ms (baseline currently ~12ms in many queues)\- quantile weighting: use P95 or P99 as the driver; tests: f(q) linear vs log mapping (e.g., f = 1 + alpha*(q95/target95), alpha in {0.5,1.0,1.5})\- sliding window sizes: 30s, 2m, 5m (tradeoff between stability and responsiveness)\- fairshare budget: budget_size {5,10,20} batch-equivalents, replenish_rate {1/100ms, 1/200ms, 1/500ms}\- budget consumption model: proportional to estimated tokens vs binary per-request

Instrumentation/metrics to capture
- Request level: arrival timestamp, priority, estimated tokens, queue_id, chosen timeout, batch_id (if formed), time to dispatch, time to first token generated\- Aggregates: per-minute P50/P90/P95/P99/P999 latencies, mean batch size, fraction of requests served within base_timeout, preemption frequency, queue occupancy percentiles, budget depletion events by class\- Cost proxies: tokens generated per-second per-queue, kernel utilization (GPU occupancy), average request token length

Early simulation outputs (notes)
- Replay of 2025-01-07 production sample (10% sample) indicates that annealing using P95 with alpha=1.0 and base_timeout=12ms reduces simulated P99 for P0 class by ~18% and increases mean token throughput by -1.6% (i.e., slight drop) — acceptable tradeoff.
- Using P99 as driver is too noisy with 30s windows; 2m windows stabilize but respond slower to burst onset.\- Fairshare budget of size 10 with replenish 1/200ms prevented a simulated starvation event where P2 bulk traffic monopolized slots for ~140s. Preemption count dropped 48% in that trace.

Observed risks and open questions
- Stability: oscillations if annealing too reactive -> risk of timeout thrash. Need hysteresis or minimum hold time after changing timeouts.
- Metric signal lag: using small sliding windows leads to noise; larger windows slow reaction. Tradeoffs need more sims.
- Customer impact: minted timeouts may change token cost subtly; need to ensure premium customers (dedicated) aren't negatively impacted by shared sched decisions. Consider per-tenant overrides.

Implementation notes / engineering tasks
- telemetry: add quantile collector component in scheduler agent (lightweight, ring-buffer summary) — PR stub at linked_artifacts PR/842.
- scheduler: implement T_q computation as pluggable policy with config knobs for alpha, base_timeout, window_size. Add min/max clamp and hold-time.
- fairshare allocator: simple token-bucket per-priority in scheduler loop; expose metrics and debug traces.
- testing: unit tests for annealing math, chaos test sim that flips workload mix.

Acceptance criteria for rollout
- P99 for latency-sensitive routes decreases by >=10% on average across test cohort with 95% confidence at A/B test significance (stat test TBD).\- Overall tokens-per-second across fleet changes <= 5%; cost proxy stable.
- No increase in tail error rates or timeouts >2x baseline.

Immediate next steps (short-term)
- Liam: finish quantile collector sim (due 2025-01-21)\- Priya: flesh out canary rollout plan and rollback criteria, coordinate with production SRE (due 2025-01-24)\- Diego: prototype fairshare allocator in local scheduler branch and add debug events (due 2025-01-20)\- Maya (owner): run initial replay sim, produce plot of P99 vs base_timeout/alpha matrix (deliver 2025-01-18)

Notes to self / loose thoughts
- Consider giving short latency-sensitive requests a small "fastpath" hint that bypasses annealing if they arrive with small token estimate (<8 tokens).\- For Dedicated customers, expose an opt-in policy toggle: "strict latency mode" that pins timeouts and disables fairshare.
- If oscillations persist, explore simple PID dampeners on timeout adjustments or using EWMA of quantiles instead of raw quantiles.

References and links
- See PR: serving-runtime/pull/842 (quantile collector)\- Trace sample used: s3://prod-traces/2025-01-sample-10pct.gz (internal)

Unresolved
- exact statistical test for A/B (t-test not ideal for tail metrics) — propose using bootstrap of P99 samples or percentile bootstrap.
- how to correlate kernel-level GPU stalls with high-level queue preemption — need to add a mapping tag in traces.

Finished? No — this is the working doc. Expect iterative updates as sims complete and canary data arrives.
